name: Reserve ratio
seoTitle: Reserve ratio Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Reserve ratio: work out reserves from the loanable funds and the reserve ratio. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: reserves is what the Reserve ratio calculator works out, and it gets there from the loanable funds and the reserve ratio. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Reserve ratio calculator work?
sections.html:
The Reserve ratio calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports reserves in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the loanable funds and the reserve ratio.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Reserve ratio calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Reserves=deposits × reserve ratio
Reserves=deposits − loanable funds

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Deposits = 10 and Reserve ratio = 10 %. The calculator returns Reserves = 1 and Loanable funds = 9.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Reserves = 1 and Loanable funds = 9 should be roughly the size you expected from Deposits = 10 and Reserve ratio = 10 %.

sections.html:

  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Reserve ratio calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the loanable funds and the reserve ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Reserve ratio calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Reserve ratio calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns reserves, derived from the loanable funds and the reserve ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Reserve ratio calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the loanable funds and the reserve ratio, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter deposits in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Deposits opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Reserves = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Reserve ratio calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
